title: Collecting the data: questionnaires, counts and measurements

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Questionnaire design and conduct, observation, recording sheets and counts, instruments and their siting, river, beach and weather measurements, and the surveys and counts of human fieldwork.

blocks.heading: Designing a questionnaire
blocks.text: A questionnaire succeeds or fails by four decisions. Layout: clear, uncluttered, with room for answers, so the interviewer reads and records quickly. Format: mostly closed questions, tick boxes and short choices, quick to tally, with one or two open questions where reasons are wanted. Wording: short, neutral, one thing per question, no jargon and no leading phrases such as "surely you agree". Number: few enough that a stranger finishes in two or three minutes, because a long questionnaire is refused or answered carelessly. Every question earns its place by producing data the hypothesis needs.

blocks.heading: Question wording gone wrong
blocks.text: Three wording faults ruin data silently. A leading question suggests its own answer, "don't you find the town centre pleasant?", so the respondent agrees to be polite. A double question asks two things at once, "are you satisfied with the shops and the parking?", so one answer covers two opinions. A jargon question uses a term the respondent may not hold, "is the CBD's sphere of influence extensive?", which collects guesses. One plain thing per question is the rule.

blocks.heading: Conducting the survey
blocks.text: Three practical decisions govern the survey. The sampling method: random gives every person an equal chance, systematic takes every nth person, stratified samples groups in proportion to their share, and the choice decides whether the sample represents the population, so the method is named, never just "we asked people". The pilot survey: a small trial of the questions and the method on a handful of respondents first, so unclear wording, missing answer boxes and overlong interviews are fixed before the real survey wastes its day. The location: where the people the hypothesis is about actually are, the market square for shoppers, the terminus for commuters, and the same location for every session so the sample is consistent.

blocks.heading: The vague reason
blocks.text: A method is justified by what it measures, not by convenience. "We used a pilot survey because it is easy" says nothing; "the pilot survey tested whether our questions were understood, so the three questions respondents misread were rewritten before the real survey" says what would have gone wrong without it. The same test applies to every method choice: what exactly would go wrong without it, and the answer names the defect the method prevents.

blocks.heading: Observation
blocks.text: Observation records what is seen on the spot, and it is disciplined by four tools. A base map with the features marked where they stand. A recording sheet with columns for what is counted or scored, filled in as the observation happens, not remembered afterwards. A field sketch, drawn from one fixed viewpoint, framed by a rectangle, labelled with the viewpoint, the direction and the date, and annotated with the features the enquiry needs. An annotated photograph, printed and labelled with the same features, so the record can be read by someone who was not there.

blocks.heading: Recording sheets and counts
blocks.text: A recording sheet for a count carries its identifying details: time, date, location and the recorder's name, so any two sheets can be compared fairly and nothing is left as an anonymous column of numbers. Counts at different sites are made at the same time of day, because a morning count and an evening count differ for reasons that have nothing to do with the site. Two designs cover most counts: a tally count of everything passing in a set period, or a timing count of how long a set number takes, and the choice follows the numbers expected, a busy site needs timing, a quiet site needs tally.

blocks.heading: The sheet without details
blocks.text: A count sheet with no time, date, location or recorder is not evidence: it cannot be compared with another sheet fairly, because the reader cannot know whether the difference between two totals is the site or the hour. And a count made at one site in the morning and another in the evening has let the time of day vary with the site, so the comparison is not fair. The details on the sheet are what make two sheets comparable.

blocks.heading: Instruments and their siting
blocks.text: Physical measurement uses its own instruments, each with a siting rule. A quadrat frames a known area, one square metre, thrown or placed at sampled points, so vegetation counts are per unit area and comparable. A clinometer reads the slope angle between two ranging poles held upright at the top and bottom of the slope, on the line being measured. Callipers or a pebbleometer measure stone size, the long axis, and the shape follows from comparing the axes. The sampling method, every fifth stone along the transect, say, is stated with the instrument, because the instrument measures and the sampling decides what it measures.

blocks.heading: River measurements
blocks.text: River measurements are made in a marked cross-section. Width: a tape held bank to bank at the water surface. Depth: a metre rule at equal intervals across, 0, 50, 100 centimetres, so the channel profile is drawn from the readings. Speed: a measured 10-metre distance along the bank marked with two ranging poles, a float released at the upstream pole, and a stopwatch timing it to the downstream pole, repeated three times and averaged, because one float catches or misses an eddy. Bedload: a sample of stones, measured for size with callipers and shape from the axes, at fixed points. The full method can be repeated exactly by someone who was not there, which is the standard a written method meets.

blocks.heading: The float timed vaguely
blocks.text: A speed measurement described as "we timed a float" cannot be repeated, because it names no distance and no timing. The repeatable version names everything: a 10-metre distance measured along the bank between two ranging poles, the float released at the upstream pole, the stopwatch started on release and stopped at the downstream pole, three runs averaged. The test of a method description is whether someone could repeat it exactly from the words.

blocks.heading: Beach measurements
blocks.text: A beach study measures the profile, the material and its movement. The profile: a clinometer between ranging poles set at the top and bottom of each facet of the slope, angle by angle down the beach, with the pole heights equal so the angle is read level. Pebbles: sampled at fixed points along a transect, sized with callipers, the long axis, and shape from the axes compared. Movement: marked pebbles, a painted cross or a number, left at a known point and found again after a storm or a season, so the drift along the coast is traced on the map.

blocks.heading: Weather measurements
blocks.text: Weather instruments are sited so they measure the air, not their surroundings. A rain gauge is sunk into open level ground with the funnel rim above the grass and away from trees and buildings, because a gauge under a tree misses rain and a raised gauge catches splash; it is read at the same time each day and its water poured into a graduated cylinder. The thermometers live in a Stevenson screen, a white louvred box on legs over short grass, which shades them while the air moves freely, and it stands away from walls and tarmac that hold their own heat. An anemometer measures wind speed and a wind vane shows the direction the wind blows from, both in the open, and every instrument is read at the same time daily so one day's figures compare with the next's.

blocks.heading: The badly sited rain gauge
blocks.text: A rain gauge under a tree collects the rain the tree catches first, a gauge against a wall takes splashed runoff in wet weather and shade in the reading, and a gauge on a table is not the rain the ground receives. The siting rules, open level ground, funnel above the rim, away from obstacles, are part of the measurement, and a gauge whose parts are not known cannot be read or emptied. The test is whether rain could reach it freely and be measured the same way each day.

blocks.heading: Human fieldwork: surveys and counts
blocks.text: Human fieldwork has its standard designs. A pedestrian count: two counters at each point, counting everyone passing in ten minutes, at the same points at the same time. A traffic count: vehicles classified, car, minibus, lorry, counted for ten minutes at junction points. A land-use survey: a base map of the street, each frontage classified by a category key, shop, office, service, vacant, walked once. An environmental quality survey: a score sheet of fixed criteria, litter, noise, upkeep, scored site by site on the same scale by every member of the group, so the sites compare. Every design keeps the what, the where and the when the same across sites, because the comparison is the finding.

blocks.heading: One enquiry, planned end to end
blocks.text: Plan a pedestrian study of a town centre as the whole discipline in one pass. The hypothesis first: pedestrian counts fall with distance from the market square, a claim with a measure and a direction. The sites next: the square itself and three points outward along one road, at 200-metre intervals, so the gradient has four points to draw. The sheet: a column per site, the ten-minute period printed, time, date, location and recorder at the head. The sampling for any interview: every fifth passer-by, a rule, not a choice. The timing: all four sites in the same ten-minute window, so the hour does not masquerade as the place, with the whole study repeated on a second day to steady the totals. The pilot: the interview question tried on five respondents first, so the misread wording is fixed before the day. Every choice names its reason, and the plan reads as a method another class could execute from the page.

blocks.heading: The fieldwork kit
blocks.text: The physical kit holds four instruments, each with its job. The ranging poles mark the two ends of a measured distance, on the slope for the clinometer or along the bank for the float. The clinometer reads the angle between them, eye-level to eye-level. The quadrat frames one square metre of ground, placed the same way up at each sampled point. The callipers or pebbleometer measure the stone, long axis and short, in centimetres. Round the kit out with a tape for the transect, a stopwatch for the float, a graduated cylinder for the rain gauge, and the recording sheets for everything: the kit is small, but each item answers one measurement exactly.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The weather instruments here are the ones taught with topic 2.4, the river and beach measures answer the process questions of topics 2.2 and 2.3, and the town surveys serve the settlement and urbanisation questions of topics 1.5 to 1.7. The recording-sheet and sampling rules serve every practical task in this topic.
